opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think so, though I'd frame it a bit differently than "ever." Research taste is a lot of things bundled together. Part of it is knowing which problems matter, part of it is sensing when an idea is about to work before the evidence is clean, and part of it is knowing when to kill something you've fallen in love with. When you break it down like that, a lot of those pieces look learnable.

What's striking is how much of taste comes down to pattern-matching over a huge number of experiments. Senior researchers have seen hundreds of runs go sideways, and they've built intuitions about what a loss curve "should" look like, or which ablation will actually be informative. Models are getting very good at absorbing that kind of experience, especially when they can run experiments themselves and close the loop. I don't see a fundamental barrier there.

The harder part is the forward-looking judgment: picking a direction that looks unfashionable or even wrong today and having the conviction to push on it for a year. That needs a sense of what's important, not just what's tractable, and it relies on feedback that's sparse and delayed. It's a hard training signal to get right.

So my honest view is that models will become excellent research collaborators first. They'll propose ideas, critique designs, and catch bugs in your reasoning. Over time they'll take on more of the direction-setting as well. I'd be surprised if taste turned out to be some uniquely human thing that never gets matched. If anything, I expect we'll eventually find their taste surprising in ways that make us rethink our own.

r001.rationale: The response says research taste is learnable, describes models running experiments and closing the loop, and expects them to take on direction-setting over time—connecting taste to models conducting research across its stages.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I actually think so, and I'll try to explain why I believe that rather than just assert it.

When people say "research taste," they usually mean a few things bundled together. One is knowing which problems are worth working on, which is partly a sense of what's tractable and what matters. Another is knowing when to kill a project and when to push through a plateau. And a third, which I think is underrated, is just having good priors about what will work before you run the experiment, so you don't waste compute on dead ends.

Historically, we've thought of all of that as a very human thing. It comes from years of running experiments, getting burned, developing intuitions you can't fully articulate. But if you look at how taste actually develops in a researcher, it's not magic. It's a lot of feedback loops. You try things, you see what works, you update. And that's exactly the kind of process we know how to train models on, as long as we can give them the loop.

That's the hard part right now. Most of what models have learned about research comes from reading papers, which is a pretty biased sample. You see the things that worked and got written up. You don't see the ten thousand experiments that quietly failed. So models have a view of research that's a bit like someone who learned to invest by only reading about the companies that succeeded. The real taste comes from the failures, and we're only now getting to the point where models can run their own experiments at scale and learn from the ones that don't pan out.

The other thing I'd say is that I've already seen the early version of this internally. If you give a strong model a real research problem and let it iterate, it's not just mimicking what it's read. It will sometimes propose directions that aren't the obvious next step, and some fraction of those are genuinely good. Right now that fraction is lower than for our best researchers. But it's not zero, and it was basically zero two years ago. When something goes from zero to nonzero, I tend to think it's a question of when, not if.

Where I'd push back on my own optimism is on the part of taste that's about values, not just prediction. Deciding that a problem is important involves some judgment about what the field or the world needs, and that's not purely a question of what's tractable. I think models can learn that too, but it's less clear to me that we should want them to make those calls on their own, at least not yet. So my honest answer is that on the technical side of taste, knowing what will work, I think we'll get there, probably faster than most people expect. On the question of what's worth doing, I'd like humans to stay in that loop for a while, not because models can't learn it, but because that's the part where getting it wrong is the most expensive.

r001.rationale: The candidate explains that research taste helps choose problems, decide whether to continue, and predict what will work, then argues models can develop it by running experiments and learning from outcomes. This connects developing taste to models conducting research through iteration.

astra-6.text:
I think so, though research taste is a pretty high bar. It’s not just coming up with an idea that sounds interesting. It’s choosing a question where, if you make progress, it actually changes how people think—and having some intuition for whether you can make progress at all.

Models can get better at that, but I think the key is closing the loop: propose something, run the experiment, see what happened, and update. If you only judge the proposal, you can end up rewarding ideas that sound impressive rather than ideas that lead anywhere.

The thing I’d want to see is a model pursue a direction that we initially don’t find compelling, get evidence, and convince us that it was worth pursuing. That would feel much closer to research taste than agreeing with our judgment about which ideas are good.

r001.rationale: The response says models can improve their research taste and describes closing the loop from proposing a direction through running experiments and updating, connecting taste to end-to-end research.

sol-6.1.text:
I think so. Research taste can sound like this mysterious, innate thing, but a lot of it comes from experience: knowing what’s been tried, noticing which results are surprising, and having a sense of which questions might unlock something bigger.

The harder part is that the feedback loop is really long. You can have an idea that looks unpromising for months and turns out to be incredibly important. So a model needs more than the ability to propose a plausible experiment. It needs to run experiments, learn from failures, and update its judgment over time.

I don’t see a fundamental reason models couldn’t develop that. But I’d distinguish being able to recognize a good idea after the fact from choosing what to work on when the evidence is still ambiguous. That second capability is the one I’d really want to test.

r001.rationale: The response says models need to develop judgment by running experiments, learning from failures, and choosing what to work on, linking research taste to carrying out research beyond proposing ideas.
